durst: dared; an old past-tense form of 'dare'
aduasoy: a heavy, glossy silk fabric used for dresses
blind: a window screen or shade, usually of cloth or wood
crochet: needlework made by looping thread with a hooked needle
decanters: glass bottles, usually stoppered, for holding wine or spirits
dragoon: a cavalry soldier who fought on horseback
dessert: the sweet course served at the end of a formal meal
elder: older, senior; used of the older of two people
forrard: a dialect form of 'forward', meaning eager or bold
gentility: respectable social rank, marked by refined manners and behaviour
jockey-cap: a small close-fitting cap like those worn by racehorse riders
lordship: a title of respect used when addressing or speaking of a lord
mammy: a childish or dialect word for mother or a nurse
maiden: an unmarried woman, often an older lady who never married
ostentatious: showy and designed to attract admiration or attention
pasture: grassy land where cattle or sheep graze
penitent: feeling sorry and ashamed for having done wrong
preserves: fruit cooked with sugar to make jam or jelly
prophetess: a woman who claims to foretell future events
sotto: in a low voice, so that others cannot hear
sonorous: deep, full and resonant in sound
stringent: strict and demanding, with rules that must be obeyed
stately: dignified, grand and impressive in appearance or manner
silks: fine, costly fabrics woven from silk thread
tenor: the general course, drift or meaning of something
vulgar: in old usage, common, coarse or in bad taste
wistfully: sadly and longingly, as if wishing for something unattainable
yeoman: a small landowner who farmed his own land
uncouth: awkward, clumsy and rough in manner
strong-minded: independent, determined and not easily influenced by others
economy: careful management of money, avoiding unnecessary spending
affrighted: frightened or terrified, an old form of 'frightened'
counting-house: an office where a business keeps its accounts and records
invalid: a person who is ill or disabled and needs care
intelligence: news or information, especially of recent events
shopman: a male assistant who serves customers in a shop
chamber: an old word for a bedroom or private room
beguile: pass time pleasantly, or charm someone into doing something
homely: in British usage, plain, simple and not especially attractive
finery: showy, fashionable clothes and decorative ornaments
exhortation: a strong urging or earnest appeal to do something
endorsed: wrote a note or signature on the back of a document
carter: a man who drives a cart for carrying goods
ghostly: resembling a ghost; pale, spectral or unearthly
sermon: a speech on a religious or moral subject given in church
hostess: a woman who receives and entertains guests in her home
aristocratic: belonging to the upper class of noble birth and high rank
genteel: polite and refined, showing the manners of good society
rector: the clergyman in charge of a parish church
parish: a local district with its own church and clergyman
ambler: a horse that moves by lifting both legs on one side together
daresay: an informal way of saying 'I suppose' or 'I expect'
maid-servant: a female servant who does household work in a home
housekeeper: a woman employed to manage the household of a large home
irritable: easily annoyed, impatient and quick to show irritation
waist: the narrow part of the body between chest and hips, or of a dress
candle: a stick of wax with a wick, used to give light
missus: an informal or dialect word for a wife or mistress of a house
bonnet: a hat tied under the chin, worn by women in earlier times
